topics.title: Living Things
topics.description: BIO 101 Living Things, from the chapter 1–7 notes.

lessons.title: What living things are and how they stay alive
lessons.objective: List the characteristics of life and explain cells, energy, nutrition, respiration, and excretion in plain language.

blocks.text: Understand the idea

The earth holds living and non-living things. Living things have life: they are made of cells, use energy, respond, grow, reproduce, and finally die. A tree does not walk away when you touch it, but it is still alive because those life processes run inside it.

A cell is the basic unit of life. It has protoplasm inside a plasma membrane. Plant cells also have a cell wall, a large central vacuole, and chloroplasts. Animals are motile heterotrophs without a cell wall. Plants are non-motile autotrophs with a cell wall. Bacteria are prokaryotes: they have no nucleus.

Energy comes from photosynthesis or from breaking food in respiration to make ATP. Anabolism builds complex molecules. Catabolism breaks them. Together they are metabolism. Autotrophs make food; heterotrophs eat plants or animals. Living things also remove wastes by excretion.
Photosynthesis: carbon dioxide and water become glucose and oxygen in the light, using chlorophyll. Respiration then releases energy from that glucose inside cells.
blocks.title: Energy in, energy out

blocks.text: Breathing air is not the whole of respiration. Respiration is the release of energy from food in cells, with or without oxygen.
blocks.title: Respiration is not only breathing

blocks.text: What to remember

items: Life signs: organisation, energy, metabolism, growth, response, reproduction, death.
Anabolism builds; catabolism breaks; metabolism is both.
Autotrophs make food; herbivores, carnivores, and omnivores consume it.

blocks.question: Which pair is correct?
options: Anabolism breaks molecules and releases energy
Catabolism builds proteins from simpler parts
blocks.explanation: Metabolism is the name for both building (anabolism) and breaking (catabolism). Plants and animals both metabolise.

blocks.text: Recap

Living things are cellular, use energy, metabolise, grow, respond, reproduce, and die. Know plant versus animal cells, autotroph versus heterotroph, and the difference between photosynthesis and respiration.

lessons.title: Living versus non-living things
lessons.objective: Compare living and non-living things using reproduction, growth, response, movement, and death.

blocks.text: Understand the idea

Once you know the signs of life, you can sort anything you see. Living things reproduce, grow, sense stimuli, metabolise, respire, and die. Non-living things do not do these on their own. A phone can ‘move’ if you throw it, but it does not move itself, feed, or make offspring.

Reproduction may be sexual (two gametes form a zygote) or asexual (one parent: binary fission, budding, vegetative propagation). Growth is more cells or bigger cells. Animals use stem cells; plants use meristems. Organisms detect change with receptors. Plants show nastic movement rather than walking.
Every living thing has a lifespan. Senescence is biological ageing that ends in death. Non-living objects have no lifespan in this biological sense.
Humans, goats, maize, and insects are living. Rock, a pen, a building, and a charger are non-living.
blocks.title: Quick sort

blocks.text: Movement alone does not prove life. Wind moves dust. Ask also: does it grow, respire, and reproduce?
blocks.title: Do not use one sign only

blocks.text: What to remember

items: Living: life, reproduction, food/air/water, stimuli, metabolism, growth, lifespan, self-movement, respiration.
Non-living: none of those requirements.
Sexual reproduction uses two parents; asexual uses one.

blocks.question: Which statement about non-living things is true in this course?
blocks.explanation: Non-living things have no metabolism, no cell respiration, and no growth by cells. Living things do.

blocks.text: Recap
Use a checklist, not a single clue. If it cannot grow, respire, respond, or reproduce, treat it as non-living, even if it looks busy.

topics.title: Classification of Living Things
topics.description: BIO 101 Classification of Living Things, from the chapter 1–7 notes.

lessons.title: Taxonomy and the hierarchy of life
lessons.objective: Explain why we classify organisms and recite the ranks from kingdom to species.

blocks.text: Understand the idea

Classification arranges living things into groups by similarities and differences. Biologists have named more than 1.8 million kinds, and more wait to be found. Without a shared system we could not identify or talk about them clearly.

Aristotle made an early attempt. Carolus Linnaeus built the method still used to name species. Taxonomy (or systematics) is the study of those principles. Shared important features make a large group; smaller differences split that group again and again.

The ranks from largest to smallest are kingdom, phylum (or division in plants), class, order, family, genus, and species. A species is the smallest unit: members look alike in general and can mate to give fertile offspring. The scientific name has two parts: genus then species.
Humans sit in family Hominidae. The genus is the first half of the two-part name; the species is the second half.
blocks.title: Where you sit in the ladder

blocks.text: Going down the ladder does not add random labels. Variety shrinks: a kingdom is mixed, a species is tightly related.
blocks.title: Ranks are not equal

blocks.text: What to remember

items: Taxonomy = principles of classification.
Kingdom → phylum/division → class → order → family → genus → species.
Species members can breed and produce fertile young.

blocks.question: What is the smallest unit of classification?
blocks.explanation: Species is the most exact rank. Individuals can mate and produce fertile offspring.

blocks.text: Recap
We classify to name and group life. Learn Linnaeus, the seven ranks, and the two-part species name. That ladder is the map for the five kingdoms that follow.

lessons.title: Kingdom Monera
lessons.objective: Describe prokaryotes in Kingdom Monera, including bacteria and cyanobacteria.

blocks.text: Understand the idea
This course uses five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, and Animalia. Kingdoms are sorted by how they get food, what their cells are like, and whether they are one cell or many.

Monera are prokaryotes. They have no nuclear membrane. The cell wall is present and is not cellulose. They are unicellular and may be autotrophic or heterotrophic. Bacteria and blue-green algae (cyanobacteria) such as Nostoc and Spirulina belong here.

A typical bacterium has a capsule, cell wall, plasma membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, and a nucleoid of DNA. Pili are short surface strands; flagella are long and used for movement. Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall. Cyanobacteria photosynthesise but still have no mitochondria, Golgi, chloroplasts, or ER.
Draw a rod: outer capsule, then wall, then membrane, DNA tangled in the middle, ribosomes as dots, and one long flagellum.
blocks.title: Bacterial cell sketch

blocks.text: Cyanobacteria look a bit like algae, but they are prokaryotes, so they sit in Monera, not Protista or Plantae.
blocks.title: Do not file them as plants

blocks.text: What to remember

items: Monera = prokaryotic, unicellular, no nuclear membrane.
Nutrition may be autotrophic or heterotrophic.
Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic prokaryotes.

blocks.question: Which feature belongs to Kingdom Monera?
blocks.explanation: Monera are prokaryotes: the nuclear membrane is absent. They are unicellular and their wall is not cellulose.

blocks.text: Recap
Monera are the prokaryote kingdom. Remember the bacterial parts, the missing nucleus, and why blue-green algae were moved here.

lessons.title: Kingdom Protista
lessons.objective: Describe protists as early eukaryotes and give examples of movement, nutrition, and disease.

blocks.text: Understand the idea

Protista comes from a Greek word meaning ‘the very first’. These organisms are eukaryotes: they have a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Most are unicellular. Many live in water, soil, or damp places. They are treated as the first eukaryotic forms, before plants, animals, and fungi.

Some protists make their own food; others feed on other organisms. A few are multicellular. Giant kelp can grow taller than 100 feet. Kelp forests can shelter otters, and otters eat sea urchins that would otherwise destroy the kelp. That is a living partnership.

Movement may use cilia, flagella, or pseudopodia. Trypanosoma is a parasitic protist that causes sleeping sickness. Reproduction is usually asexual; sexual reproduction is rare and often happens under stress.
If you see a single-celled organism with a true nucleus in pond water, start with Protista, not Monera.
blocks.title: Pond-water test

blocks.text: Not every protist is harmless or microscopic. Some cause disease, and kelp is a huge multicellular protist.
blocks.title: Watch the exceptions

blocks.text: What to remember

items: Protists are eukaryotes, usually unicellular, often aquatic.
Nutrition: autotrophic or heterotrophic.
Trypanosoma causes sleeping sickness.

blocks.question: Which organism is a parasitic protist named in this chapter?
blocks.explanation: Trypanosoma is a protozoan that can cause sleeping sickness. Nostoc and Spirulina are cyanobacteria; yeast is a fungus.

blocks.text: Recap
Protists are the eukaryotic ‘first’ kingdom: mostly one cell, true nucleus, mixed nutrition, and several ways to move. Know kelp and Trypanosoma as named examples.

lessons.title: Fungi, plants, and animals
lessons.objective: Compare Kingdoms Fungi, Plantae, and Animalia using cell wall, food, and movement.

blocks.text: Understand the idea

Fungi include yeasts, moulds, and mushrooms. They are eukaryotic, non-motile heterotrophs. They have a cell wall and make chitin. They do not photosynthesise. They reproduce with spores, sexually or asexually, and some are parasites. They have no embryo; a spore grows into the fungus.

Kingdom Plantae holds the plants: eukaryotic, multicellular autotrophs. Chlorophyll in plastids captures light. Cells have a wall and a large central vacuole. Plants do not walk. They reproduce sexually or by vegetative propagation. Roots, stems, and leaves divide jobs such as anchorage, support, and photosynthesis.

Kingdom Animalia is the largest of the five. Animals are multicellular eukaryotes without chlorophyll or a cell wall, so they must eat. Body plan splits them into phyla such as Porifera, Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Annelida, Arthropoda, Mollusca, Echinodermata, and Chordata.
Mushroom on dead wood = fungus (absorbs food). Maize in a field = plant (makes food). Goat = animal (eats plants).
blocks.title: Three kingdoms on a farm

blocks.text: A green colour does not make an organism a plant. Cyanobacteria are green and prokaryotic. Fungi are never photosynthetic in this chapter.
blocks.title: Colour is not the kingdom

blocks.text: What to remember

items: Fungi: heterotrophs, spores, chitin, no chlorophyll.
Plants: autotrophs, chlorophyll, wall, vacuole, non-motile.
Animals: heterotrophs, no wall, no chlorophyll, many phyla.

blocks.question: Why are fungi not placed in Plantae in this course?
options: They lack chlorophyll and cannot photosynthesise
blocks.explanation: Fungi are eukaryotic heterotrophs without chlorophyll. Plants make food with chlorophyll. Fungi may be unicellular (yeast) or filamentous.

blocks.text: Recap
After Monera and Protista, sort the rest by food and cell wall: fungi absorb, plants photosynthesise, animals ingest. Learn one clear example of each.

topics.title: Cell Types and Cell Theory
topics.description: BIO 101 Cell Types and Cell Theory, from the chapter 1–7 notes.

lessons.title: The cell and cell theory
lessons.objective: Define the cell, retell how it was discovered, and state the three points of cell theory.

blocks.text: Understand the idea

The cell is the lowest living structure that can carry out life’s jobs. It is the structural and functional unit of life. Most cells are 1–100 micrometres wide. Unicellular examples are Amoeba, Paramecium, and Chlamydomonas. Multicellular examples are humans, cats, and Spirogyra. All must take in nutrients, remove wastes, respond, and reproduce.

Robert Hooke improved a compound microscope in 1665 and saw tiny pores in cork. He named them cells because they looked like monastery rooms, and he published Micrographia. Leeuwenhoek’s simple microscope magnified 200–300 times; he saw bacteria and protozoa (‘animalcules’) and described sperm in 1677.

Schleiden (plants, 1838) and Schwann (animals, 1839) argued that cells make up plants and animals. They were wrong about how new cells appear. Rudolf Virchow stated in 1855 that all cells come from existing cells. Cell theory now has three points: living things are made of cells; the cell is the smallest unit of a living thing; new cells come from pre-existing cells.
Cork looked empty to Hooke because those plant cells were dead walls. Living cells are filled with cytoplasm and organelles.
blocks.title: Why cork looked like boxes

blocks.text: Schleiden and Schwann get credit for the cell as a unit, not for cell origin. Virchow added ‘cells from cells’.
blocks.title: Split the credit

blocks.text: What to remember

items: Hooke named cells (1665); Leeuwenhoek saw microbes.
Schleiden and Schwann proposed cell theory; Virchow added origin from existing cells.
Unicellular = one cell; multicellular = many specialised cells.

blocks.question: Cell theory says new cells come from which source?
blocks.explanation: Virchow’s point is that all new cells come from cells that already exist. Schleiden’s ‘seeding’ and Schwann’s ‘crystallising’ were rejected.

blocks.text: Recap
A cell is life’s unit. Microscopes revealed it. Cell theory’s three lines are your exam core: composition, smallest unit, and origin from other cells.

lessons.title: Levels of cell organisation
lessons.objective: Order chemical, cell, tissue, organ, and system levels and give a human example of each.

blocks.text: Understand the idea

Cells did not appear fully modern. Early Earth may have received small molecules from meteorites, deep-sea vents, or lightning. RNA is often thought to be an early self-copying molecule because it can store information and speed reactions. Lipid molecules can form tiny bags in water, a step toward membranes. Cells are thought to be at least 4.0–4.3 billion years old.

Inside a body, organisation climbs. The chemical level is atoms and molecules such as amino acids. The cellular level is the working unit, including specialised cells such as egg, sperm, muscle, and nerve cells. A tissue is a group of cells with one job. Humans have epithelial, muscle, nervous, and connective tissues.

An organ is two or more tissues doing one function (heart, liver, kidney). A system is organs with a shared job: digestive, nervous, endocrine, circulatory, respiratory, urinary, reproductive. Cellular physiology is activity inside the cell; organ physiology is how organs work together.
Stomach wall: several muscle layers plus glands. That is tissue stacked into an organ, which then sits in the digestive system.
blocks.title: From tissue to system

blocks.text: Do not skip ranks. A heart is not a tissue and a cell is not an organ. Each level is built from the one below.
blocks.title: Keep the ladder

blocks.text: What to remember

items: Chemical → cell → tissue → organ → system.
Four human tissues: epithelial, muscle, nervous, connective.
Organ = two or more tissues; system = organs with one function.

blocks.question: What is an organ in this chapter?
options: Two or more tissues with a particular function
blocks.explanation: An organ is two or more tissues performing a particular function, such as heart, liver, or kidney.

blocks.text: Recap
Life likely started with simple molecules and membranes. In the body, molecules build cells, cells build tissues, tissues build organs, and organs build systems.

lessons.title: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
lessons.objective: Contrast prokaryotes and eukaryotes and list the four features common to all cells.

blocks.text: Understand the idea

There are two basic cell types. Prokaryotic means ‘before a nucleus’ (bacteria). Eukaryotic means ‘true nucleus’ (plant, animal, and your body cells). Despite the gap in complexity, both types do many of the same jobs with the same kind of DNA and the same genetic code.

Every cell has four shared parts. DNA carries instructions: in a nucleoid if prokaryotic, in a membrane-bound nucleus if eukaryotic. A plasma membrane of phospholipid and protein controls what enters. Cytoplasm is the material inside, with fluid cytosol. Ribosomes build proteins.

Eukaryotic cells are larger (about 5–100 μm) and have linear DNA with histones, several chromosomes, and membrane organelles such as mitochondria and ER. Prokaryotes are smaller (about 0.1–5 μm), with circular DNA, plasmids, a nucleoid that has no membrane, smaller ribosomes, and no true membrane organelles.
A bacterium is a backpack with tools loose inside. A liver cell is a workshop with labelled rooms (nucleus, mitochondria, Golgi).
blocks.title: Rooms versus an open bag

blocks.text: A nucleoid is not a nucleus. It is only the region where DNA sits, with no envelope around it.
blocks.title: Do not rename nucleoid

blocks.text: What to remember

items: All cells: DNA, plasma membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes.
Prokaryote: no nucleus, circular DNA, small, unicellular.
Eukaryote: true nucleus, linear chromosomes, organelles.

blocks.question: Which structures are found in all cells?
blocks.explanation: The four shared features are DNA, plasma membrane, cytoplasm, and ribosomes. Nucleus and mitochondria are eukaryotic extras.

blocks.text: Recap
Start with the four shared parts, then add the nucleus test. No nucleus and circular DNA: prokaryote. True nucleus and organelles: eukaryote.

lessons.title: Plant cells, animal cells, and a short review
lessons.objective: Compare plant and animal cells and use the chapter review questions as a self-check.

blocks.text: Understand the idea

The two eukaryotic types you must compare are plant and animal cells. Plant cells are generally larger (about 10–100 μm) with a fixed rectangular shape because a cellulose wall sits outside the plasma membrane. Animal cells are smaller (about 10–30 μm) and irregular, wrapped only by a flexible plasma membrane.

Plant cells have plastids and chloroplasts, one large supporting vacuole, and a nucleus often to one side. They store starch and can make many of their own nutrients. Animal cells lack chloroplasts and a wall. Their vacuoles are small and many. The nucleus is central. They store glycogen, have more mitochondria, and typically have centrioles, centrosomes, and lysosomes.
Both have cytoplasm, ribosomes, and a nucleus. Use those shared parts as the baseline, then add wall, chloroplast, and vacuole to recognise a plant cell in a diagram.
If a diagram shows a boxy cell with a thick outline and green ovals, it is a plant cell. A round cell with many small vacuoles is animal.
blocks.title: Exam diagram habit

blocks.text: The source review asked for two features common to all cells: cytoplasm and ribosomes are accepted answers, along with DNA and membrane from the earlier list.
blocks.title: Review trap

blocks.text: What to remember

items: Plant: wall, chloroplasts, large vacuole, starch, fixed shape.
Animal: no wall, glycogen, centrioles, lysosomes, irregular shape.
Organ = two or more tissues; prokaryotes lack nuclei.

blocks.question: Which structure is present in plant cells but not in animal cells?
blocks.explanation: Chloroplasts (and the cellulose wall and large vacuole) mark plant cells. Ribosomes, nucleus, and plasma membrane occur in both.

blocks.text: Recap
Eukaryotic does not mean identical. Plant versus animal is a table of wall, chloroplast, vacuole, stored food, and shape. That table plus cell theory closes Chapter 4.

topics.title: Activities Within the Cell
topics.description: BIO 101 Activities Within the Cell, from the chapter 1–7 notes.

lessons.title: Osmosis
lessons.objective: Define osmosis, name hypotonic, isotonic, and hypertonic solutions, and predict what happens to plant and animal cells.

blocks.text: Understand the idea

Osmosis is the movement of water (or another solvent) through a partially permeable membrane from the side with more free water to the side with less free water. That is the same as moving toward the higher solute concentration. It is passive: the cell does not spend ATP on the water flow itself.

An isotonic solution matches the cell: water in equals water out. A hypotonic solution is more dilute outside, so water enters (endosmosis); the cell becomes turgid. A hypertonic solution is more concentrated outside, so water leaves (exosmosis); the cell becomes flaccid or plasmolysed. Osmotic pressure is the pressure that can stop that flow.

Animal cells survive in isotonic fluid; they can burst (lyse) in hypotonic liquid. Plant cells have walls, so hypotonic surroundings are useful: turgor supports the plant. In isotonic solution a plant may droop. Roots take water from soil by osmosis and send it up the xylem.
Guard cells swell with water and open stomata. Freshwater fish must handle water constantly entering their cells. Cholera can reverse intestinal water flow and cause dehydration.
blocks.title: Osmosis you can notice

blocks.text: Hypotonic and hypertonic are named from solute, not from water. Hypertonic = more solute outside, so water leaves the cell.
blocks.title: Name the solute side

blocks.text: What to remember

items: Osmosis: water through a membrane, high water → low water, no extra energy.
Hypotonic: water in; hypertonic: water out; isotonic: no net change.
Plants need turgor; animal cells lyse if too much water enters.

blocks.question: What happens to an animal cell in a hypotonic solution?
options: It becomes turgid and is protected by a wall
There is no net water movement
Water enters and the cell may lyse
Water leaves and the cell plasmolyses
blocks.explanation: Hypotonic means more water enters. Animal cells lack a strong wall, so they can burst. Plant cells become turgid instead.

blocks.text: Recap
Osmosis is water following its concentration through a membrane. Link each solution name to the direction of water, then to turgor, drooping, or bursting.

lessons.title: Diffusion
lessons.objective: Define diffusion, distinguish it from osmosis, and explain simple versus facilitated diffusion.

blocks.text: Understand the idea

Diffusion is the movement of molecules from higher concentration to lower concentration until the mix is even. It happens in solids, liquids, and gases. Unlike osmosis, it does not require a membrane and both solute and solvent can move, in all directions. You cannot stop ordinary diffusion by squeezing one side.

Simple diffusion crosses a membrane or space without a helper protein, as when oxygen enters cytoplasm. Facilitated diffusion is still passive, but a carrier protein helps a substance cross from high to low concentration. Temperature, gradient steepness, distance, particle size, and membrane type change the rate.

Diffusion lets carbon dioxide leave cells, moves ions, brings soil water and minerals toward root hairs, and helps nerve signals. In plants it also moves gases through stomata and spreads flower scent. Tea in hot water, perfume in air, and incense smoke are everyday pictures of the same rule.
Osmosis is a special water story through a membrane. Diffusion is the general mixing story. If perfume fills a room, that is diffusion, not osmosis.
blocks.title: Keep the two words apart

blocks.text: Facilitated diffusion still goes high to low and does not spend ATP. Do not call it active transport.
blocks.title: Helper is not a pump

blocks.text: What to remember

items: Diffusion: high concentration → low, any state of matter.
Simple = no protein helper; facilitated = carrier, still passive.
Osmosis needs a membrane and concerns water; diffusion is broader.

blocks.question: Which statement matches diffusion rather than osmosis?
options: Only water moves, and a membrane is required
The process can be reversed by extra pressure on one side
Particles can move in all directions without a membrane
It occurs only between similar solutions
blocks.explanation: Diffusion does not need a semipermeable membrane and can run in all directions. Osmosis is the water-and-membrane case.

blocks.text: Recap
Diffusion equalises concentration. Add a membrane and water only, and you have osmosis. Add a carrier protein but no energy cost, and you have facilitated diffusion.

lessons.title: Cell division and mitosis
lessons.objective: Explain why cells divide and walk through interphase plus the stages of mitosis.

blocks.text: Understand the idea

Cell division makes new cells for growth, replacement, and reproduction. Unicellular organisms often split by binary fission. Multicellular bodies use mitosis for new body cells and meiosis for sperm and egg. Mitosis copies chromosomes so each daughter cell matches the parent. In humans that number stays 46.

The cell cycle is G1 (growth), S (DNA and centrosome copied), G2 (more growth and checks), then M phase. Interphase is G1 + S + G2, when the cell is not yet visibly dividing. M phase is prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase, then cytokinesis, which splits the cytoplasm.

In prophase the nuclear envelope breaks, the nucleolus fades, and chromosomes condense as sister chromatids. Prometaphase attaches spindle fibres to kinetochores. Metaphase lines chromosomes at the equator. Anaphase pulls sisters apart. Telophase rebuilds nuclei. Animals pinch in; plants build a cell plate.
Remember PMAT: prophase packs, metaphase meets in the middle, anaphase apart, telophase two nuclei.
blocks.title: Four letters

blocks.text: Interphase is not a rest with nothing happening. DNA is copied in S phase. If that copy is wrong, later mitosis can spread damage.
blocks.title: Interphase is busy

blocks.text: What to remember

items: Mitosis → two identical body cells; chromosome number unchanged.
Cycle: G1, S, G2, mitosis, cytokinesis.
PMAT + cytokinesis completes the visible division.

blocks.question: During which stage do sister chromatids separate?
blocks.explanation: Anaphase is the short stage when centromeres split and sisters are pulled to opposite poles. Metaphase only lines them up.

blocks.text: Recap
Mitosis keeps chromosome number and identity. Learn the cycle names, then PMAT, then how plant and animal cells finish cytokinesis differently.

lessons.title: Meiosis I and meiosis II
lessons.objective: Describe how meiosis halves the chromosome number and creates genetic variety.

blocks.text: Understand the idea

Meiosis is eukaryotic cell division that makes haploid gametes. A diploid human cell has 46 chromosomes (23 pairs). After meiosis, egg or sperm has 23. Fertilisation returns the number to 46. Meiosis is two divisions after one DNA copy: meiosis I then meiosis II.

Meiosis I separates homologous pairs. In prophase I, homologues pair, form tetrads, and may swap DNA at chiasmata (crossing over). Metaphase I lines bivalents; anaphase I sends homologues to opposite poles. The two cells are already haploid for chromosome pairs, though each chromosome still has two chromatids.

Meiosis II is like a mitosis of those haploid cells: sister chromatids separate. Variety comes from crossing over in meiosis I and from random lining-up of maternal and paternal chromosomes. Humans have 23 pairs, so independent assortment alone allows over 8 million combinations.
Sperm cell precursor diagrams in the notes show pairing and crossing over in meiosis I, then a second split. Female meiosis II also forms polar bodies beside the egg.
blocks.title: Follow the diagrams

blocks.text: Do not say meiosis II halves 46 to 23. The drop from diploid to haploid is meiosis I. Meiosis II splits chromatids.
blocks.title: Which division halves pairs

blocks.text: What to remember

items: Meiosis: one DNA copy, two divisions, haploid gametes.
Meiosis I: homologues pair, cross over, then separate.
Meiosis II: sister chromatids separate.

blocks.question: When does crossing over occur?
blocks.explanation: Homologous chromosomes pair and exchange DNA in prophase I. Mitosis has no pairing of homologues and no crossing over in this course.

blocks.text: Recap
Meiosis exists so chromosome number does not double every generation, and so offspring are not copies. Pairing, crossing over, and a second split are the story.

lessons.title: Why cell division matters
lessons.objective: List the uses of cell division and contrast mitosis with meiosis in a short table.

blocks.text: Understand the idea

Cell division is required for growth, repair, and reproduction in every living creature. Unicellular organisms reproduce by binary fission. Multicellular organisms use division to make gametes and to add or replace body cells. Without control, division can contribute to cancer.

Division renews damaged cells, produces new cells from older ones, keeps a working chromosome set, and increases cell number for growth. In plants, mitosis also builds new organs and repairs wounded parts. Meiosis is the special path that halves chromosomes for sexual reproduction.

Mitosis forms genetically identical sister chromatids and two daughters with the parent number. Meiosis pairs homologues, allows crossing over, and yields four daughters with half the count. Those two outcomes must not be swapped in an exam answer.
A healing skin cut is mitosis. Making sperm is meiosis. A bacterium splitting is binary fission, still a form of division.
blocks.title: Match the job

blocks.text: Uncontrolled division is not ‘more growth’ in a healthy sense. The notes link poor regulation to serious disease such as cancer.
blocks.title: Control matters

blocks.text: What to remember

items: Uses: growth, repair, reproduction, development.
Mitosis: two identical cells, same chromosome number.
Meiosis: four haploid cells, half the number, variety.

blocks.question: Which result matches meiosis rather than mitosis?
options: Two daughters with the parent chromosome number
Four haploid cells and crossing over
A cell plate with no chromosome change
blocks.explanation: Meiosis produces haploid cells and includes pairing and crossing over. Mitosis makes two matching body cells.

blocks.text: Recap
Ask what the new cells are for. Body growth and repair point to mitosis. Gametes and halved chromosomes point to meiosis.

topics.title: Heredity
topics.description: BIO 101 Heredity, from the chapter 1–7 notes.

lessons.title: What heredity is and why it matters
lessons.objective: Define heredity and variation, and explain why genetics matters in medicine, farming, and evolution.

blocks.text: Understand the idea

Heredity is the passing of traits from parents to offspring through genes. It is easiest to see in sexual reproduction, where children resemble both parents but are not copies. Variation comes from DNA copying mistakes, from the environment acting on genes, and from mutations. Asexual offspring vary much less.

Heredity is the base of biological diversity: traits travel generation to generation and help explain why organisms look and behave as they do. It is also the foundation of genetics, which studies genes, inheritance, genetic disease, and evolution.

Knowing heredity helps diagnose genetic disorders, estimate risk, and counsel families. It underpins evolution by natural selection, crop improvement, gene therapy, and conservation of endangered species. It also raises ethical questions about testing and genetic technology.
A family may share eye colour through genes, while a farmer selects seed that keeps a useful trait in the next harvest.
blocks.title: Home and farm

blocks.text: Aristotle thought parental traits blended like paint, so a tall and short parent would make medium children forever. Mendel showed units can hide and reappear.
blocks.title: Blending is the old error

blocks.text: What to remember

items: Heredity = traits through genes from parent to offspring.
Variation is normal and fuels diversity and evolution.
Applications: medicine, biotechnology, conservation, ethics.

blocks.question: What is heredity?
options: Passing traits from parents to offspring through genes
Any change caused only by weather
The mixing of blood in Aristotle’s sense
blocks.explanation: Heredity is gene-based transmission of characteristics from one generation to the next.

blocks.text: Recap
Heredity is genetic handover. Variation keeps life diverse. That idea opens medicine, evolution, and the pea experiments in the next lesson.

lessons.title: Mendel’s experiments and genetic terms
lessons.objective: State Mendel’s main laws and use genotype, phenotype, and allele language on a monohybrid cross.

blocks.text: Understand the idea

Gregor Mendel (1822–1884), an Austrian monk, crossed pea plants and tracked height, flower colour, and seed texture. He showed that traits are discrete units (now called genes) that come in pairs (alleles) and are inherited by rules, not by blending.

The law of segregation: the two alleles for a trait separate when gametes form, so each gamete carries one. Offspring get one allele from each parent. Independent assortment: alleles for different traits segregate independently. Dominance: a dominant allele can hide a recessive allele in a heterozygote. F2 often shows about three dominant phenotypes to one recessive.

A gene is a DNA unit of inheritance. Alleles are its alternative forms. Genotype is the allele set (TT, Tt, tt). Phenotype is what you see (tall or short). Capital letters are dominant; lowercase recessive. Homozygous means both alleles the same; heterozygous means they differ. Chromosomes are the threads that carry genes.
Tall (TT or Tt) × short (tt). F1 is all tall Tt. F2 is about 3 tall : 1 short, with genotypes 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt. One T is enough for tall.
blocks.title: Monohybrid height

blocks.text: A 3:1 ratio is the phenotype in F2, not the genotype. The genotype split is 1:2:1. Dihybrid crosses follow two trait pairs at once.
blocks.title: Ratio mix-up

blocks.text: What to remember

items: Segregation, independent assortment, and dominance are Mendel’s core rules.
Genotype = alleles; phenotype = expressed trait.
Monohybrid F2 phenotype ≈ 3:1; genotype 1:2:1.

blocks.question: In a monohybrid tall × short cross, why can F2 include short plants again?
options: Because blending makes medium then short
Because recessive alleles can meet as tt after segregation
Because F1 plants were all short
blocks.explanation: F1 heterozygotes are tall. Segregation lets two t alleles meet in some F2 offspring, which are short. The trait was hidden, not destroyed.

blocks.text: Recap
Mendel turned inheritance into countable units. Learn the three laws, the letter code, and the monohybrid ratios before you read genes and chromosomes in Chapter 7.

topics.title: Genes and Chromosomes
topics.description: BIO 101 Genes and Chromosomes, from the chapter 1–7 notes.

lessons.title: Genes, DNA, and how genes work
lessons.objective: Describe genes as DNA instructions and outline transcription, translation, and gene function.

blocks.text: Understand the idea

Genes are the basic units of heredity: segments of DNA that carry instructions, especially for proteins. DNA is a double helix of two polynucleotide chains. Four bases write the code: adenine (A), cytosine (C), thymine (T), and guanine (G). About three billion bases are in a human; roughly 99% are the same in everyone.

William Bateson used ‘genetics’ in 1905. Wilhelm Johannsen named the ‘gene’ in 1909. A gene sits at a locus on a chromosome. The genome is the full set. Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes. A codon is three bases that specify an amino acid. Transcription copies a gene into mRNA; translation builds the protein.

Genes control DNA and RNA work and therefore enzymes and structures such as haemoglobin, which carries oxygen. Phenotype comes from genotype plus environment. Many traits are polygenic. Mutations create alleles; natural selection and drift change how common those alleles are.
Each parent passes one copy of a gene, so a child can show a mix of both, such as hair or eye features.
blocks.title: Why children resemble both parents

blocks.text: DNA is the stored manual; RNA can be a working copy. Do not say a gene is the whole chromosome.
blocks.title: Gene is a segment

blocks.text: What to remember

items: Gene = DNA instruction, often for a protein; locus = its place.
DNA bases A, C, T, G; codon = three bases.
Transcription then translation turn a gene into protein.

blocks.question: What is a codon in this chapter?
options: Three DNA bases that specify an amino acid
blocks.explanation: The genetic code uses three-base units (codons) to specify amino acids in a protein.

blocks.text: Recap
A gene is a DNA paragraph. Chromosomes are the books. Expression copies the paragraph into RNA and then into protein, which does the body’s work.

lessons.title: Chromosomes and their relationship to genes
lessons.objective: Explain what chromosomes are, how they differ from genes, and why chromosome errors matter.

blocks.text: Understand the idea

A chromosome is a microscopic thread of DNA plus packaging proteins. It carries many genes. In eukaryotes DNA wraps on histone proteins so a huge length can fit in the nucleus. Chromosomes become easy to see when a cell divides. Each daughter cell should receive a complete set.

A gene is a short coded stretch and is not visible under an ordinary microscope. A chromosome is a pack of many genes, visible when condensed, and large changes (duplication, deletion, inversion, rearrangement) affect many genes at once. Equal splitting of chromosomes keeps DNA balanced; unequal splitting can cause disorders.

Genes and chromosomes together transmit instructions through mitosis and meiosis, regulate when proteins are made, and sit in linked groups. Errors can cause conditions named in the notes such as Down syndrome, Turner syndrome, and some leukaemias. Understanding this map also supports gene editing, personalised medicine, and conservation.
Think of a chromosome as a necklace and genes as the beads. Moving the whole necklace is a chromosomal change; swapping one bead is a gene mutation.
blocks.title: Necklace model

blocks.text: Do not treat gene and chromosome as synonyms. Exams ask for definition, location, visibility, and size of change.
blocks.title: Use the comparison table

blocks.text: What to remember

items: Chromosome = long DNA with many genes, packed with histones.
Gene = one coded segment on a chromosome.
Chromosome mistakes can cause named genetic disorders.

blocks.question: Which statement is true?
options: A chromosome is a pack of genes visible in cell division
Genes are visible under a light microscope as X shapes
Histones are the four DNA bases
blocks.explanation: Chromosomes package many genes with proteins and are the structures you see during division. Genes themselves are not those X shapes.

blocks.text: Recap
Genes are instructions; chromosomes are the structures that carry, copy, and share those instructions. Keep that relationship clear and you have finished BIO 101 chapters 1–7.
